Name: Punic Commercial Documents: Clay Tablets, Clay Seals and the Public Law of the Notaries' Guild
RagShortTexts: Carthage's commercial network spanned the whole western Mediterranean and relied on strictly notarized clay-tablet contracts
Clay sealings in the Tyrian language recorded the grade and weight of goods, guarantees and the shipowner's oath
Merchant guild notarial courts in every port settled cross-national disputes over breach of contract
BaseText: The city-state of Carthage was in essence a vast, unrivaled commercial oligarchic trust. What kept its hundreds of ports running efficiently was a highly developed system of documentary notarization derived from ancient Phoenician commercial law. At the customs houses and dockside exchanges of each port were stationed commercial notaries (Makarim) licensed by the Council of One Hundred. Every bulk consignment, whether tin ingots from Gadir, ivory from the Sahara or wheat and oil from Sicily, had to have a detailed contract inscribed in Punic letters on a soft clay tablet, including the grade of the goods, the allowance for moisture loss, the penalty for breach, and the sacred oath the captain had sworn in the temple of Baal. The document was tied with fine linen cord, wrapped in wet clay, and sealed with a bronze or carnelian seal (Bulla). Such contract tablets were recognized in public law at the customs houses of Rome, Syracuse and Massalia, and even in wartime served as legal proof for the protection of private property and the settlement of prisoner ransoms.

Variants.Content: Swords can change hands, but the clay pattern of a seal cannot be altered! As long as the notary's clay seal is intact, whether you are a Gallic high chieftain or a Roman tribune, you must pay out the silver by the weight written on it.

The Carthaginians are as cunning as foxes, but their commercial documents truly leave no gaps. With a potsherd bearing the double-headed eagle seal of the Byrsa citadel, you can raise cash on it in any port of the Mediterranean.

The peddlers measure the world with mud-smeared potsherds, while the Romans divide their territory with the boundary stones of the legions. On the day the city falls, all their fancy ledgers will turn back into dirt!
